name: Gluconolactone

card.summary: A food-additive-turned-skincare 'PHA' that small trials suggest irritates less than glycolic acid, though the evidence base is thin.
card.note: Skin trial evidence is limited to a handful of small studies; products still carry general exfoliant sun-protection advice.

quick.overview:
Gluconolactone (glucono-delta-lactone) is an oxidised derivative of glucose, widely used as a food additive (E575). In skincare it is sold as a polyhydroxy acid, pitched at sensitive skin as a gentler alternative to glycolic acid.

Published skin studies are few. They report effects broadly comparable to alpha hydroxy acids in small comparisons, with less stinging in some, and an expert panel has judged it safe at cosmetic-use levels.
quick.mechanism: In water it partly converts to gluconic acid, so acidity develops gradually. It is described as a mild exfoliant, humectant and chelating agent, with some in-vitro data on reduced UV-induced elastin damage.
quick.risks: Cosmetic Ingredient Review concluded in 2022 it is safe at reported use concentrations, per Grokipedia. Large oral doses act as a laxative. As with other exfoliating acids, sun protection is generally advised.

lead: Gluconolactone, also called glucono-delta-lactone (GDL), is the cyclic ester of D-gluconic acid, made by oxidising glucose.[1] In skincare it is classed as a polyhydroxy acid (PHA) and used as a chemical exfoliant, humectant and antioxidant ingredient in toners, serums and peels, where it is marketed for smoother, more even-looking skin with less stinging than classic alpha hydroxy acids.[2][5]

People use gluconolactone products to loosen dead surface cells, support the skin barrier and leave skin brighter and softer, including on sensitive, rosacea-prone or acne-prone skin and after cosmetic procedures.[5][2] Its larger industrial footprint is as a food additive (E575) used as an acidifier, sequestrant and leavening or curing agent.[1][2]

Dermatologists quoted in consumer coverage describe PHAs as acclimating the skin to exfoliation with less irritation than classic acids, though they also note that PHAs can still irritate some people.[13]

The clinical literature includes a double-blind trial of 14% gluconolactone against benzoyl peroxide in 150 acne patients, review papers on PHAs in photoaged skin, and a 2025 paired study of a 5% gluconolactone serum against intense pulsed light for mild rosacea redness.[5][7][12] A cosmetic ingredient safety panel concluded that gluconolactone is safe in cosmetics in present practices of use and concentration.[4]

Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety: safe as used (2026)[4]

paras: GDL is a white, nearly odourless crystalline powder, typically produced by glucose oxidase action or fermentation of glucose.[1][2] In water it hydrolyses gradually toward gluconic acid until an equilibrium is reached, so a fresh solution grows more acidic over about two hours; heat and high pH accelerate the process.[1][2]

Brands market it for gentle exfoliation, hydration and use on sensitive or acne-prone skin.[2] A 2004 review in Cutis describes PHAs as a newer generation of AHAs that provide similar effects without the sensory irritation that can limit classical AHAs, and states that they have been found compatible with clinically sensitive skin, including rosacea and atopic dermatitis, and can be used after cosmetic procedures.[5]

The same review says PHAs provide additional humectant and moisturising properties, can strengthen stratum corneum barrier function and thereby increase resistance to chemical challenge, and mostly have antioxidant properties. It also says gluconolactone or lactobionic acid may be combined with other products or procedures such as laser and microdermabrasion.[5] Grokipedia adds that older trials classed gluconolactone as an AHA.[2]

As E575 it is used in tofu coagulation, dairy, cured meats and baking.[2] A combination of citric acid, gluconolactone and magnesium carbonate (Renacidin) is a US-labelled irrigation solution for dissolving certain bladder stones and preventing catheter encrustation.[12]

sections.h: How it works and how it compares
paras: PHAs are described as having larger molecules than the alpha and beta hydroxy acids, so they penetrate less deeply, which is the usual explanation offered for lower irritation.[13] Healthline summarises research suggesting PHAs are nearly as effective as AHAs and BHAs while causing less irritation, and notes that one 2004 study partly funded by a cosmetics company found PHAs and glycolic acid both had anti-ageing effects over 12 weeks, with PHAs being less irritating.[13][5]

Antioxidant activity is also attributed to PHAs: dermatologist Tsippora Shainhouse is quoted in that coverage as saying they may help counter UV and pollution-related damage, and dermatologist Dendy Engelman says PHAs acclimate the skin to exfoliation with little risk of irritation.[13] AHAs such as glycolic and lactic acid are used for acne, dark spots, dryness and wrinkles, but can sting and increase sun sensitivity.[13][6]

PHAs became a recurring ingredient category in consumer skincare as a gentler choice for sensitive, rosacea-prone or eczema-prone skin, appearing in cleansers, toners, pads, masks, serums and moisturisers.[13] Consumer guidance from dermatologists quoted by Healthline includes wearing broad-spectrum sunscreen during the day, patch testing, and not stacking several chemical exfoliants at once, since this can overwork the skin; the same coverage says PHAs can still irritate some people.[13]

A 1992 double-blind randomised trial in 150 patients evaluated the AHA gluconolactone at 14% for acne against benzoyl peroxide, assessing efficacy and skin tolerance.[7] According to Grokipedia, both treatments reduced lesions and fewer side effects were reported for gluconolactone; this description comes from an AI-generated summary.[2]

A 1997 randomised clinical trial in the British Journal of Dermatology studied how alpha hydroxy acids modulate stratum corneum barrier function,[8] and the 2004 Cutis review summarises studies in which PHA-containing products were combined with retinoic acid in adult facial acne and found well tolerated.[5] Grokipedia also describes a 12-week photoaging comparison with glycolic acid in which both improved features, with glycolic acid ahead on some measures and causing more stinging, and an 8% gluconolactone regimen that caused less irritation after a detergent challenge than some comparators.[2]

More recent trials include a 2025 paired-control study comparing a 5% gluconolactone-based topical serum with intense pulsed light for mild erythema of rosacea,[9] a 2018 randomised study of a novel acne combination differentiated by gender,[10] and a 2018 randomised trial of dietary glucono-delta-lactone and skin condition.[11] A registered trial of topical antioxidant agents in photodamaged skin also exists but is not specific to gluconolactone.[3]

The Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety assessed five glycolactone ingredients in a review published in 2026 and concluded that gluconolactone is safe in cosmetics in the present practices of use and concentration; it found the data insufficient for four other glycolactones.[4] Grokipedia reports an earlier 2022 conclusion of safety at the concentrations in use, including up to 15% in leave-on products, and that patch tests found no irritation or sensitisation.[2] Single oral doses above about 20 g have caused laxative effects in humans.[2]

The Renacidin label lists bladder irritation and chemical cystitis in about 3% of patients, a distinct irrigation use.[12] For AHAs generally, regulators have noted possible increased sun sensitivity.[6]

chain: Large-molecule acid loosens dead surface cells
Smoother, more even, less dull skin with little stinging
angle.text: Gluconolactone is used in toners, serums and peels as a gentler exfoliant. It is chosen by people who want smoother, brighter skin but find stronger acids such as glycolic acid too irritating.
